rubric: DATABASES / AGGREGATES, JOINS AND SUBQUERIES / CHAPTER 5

slides.title: Many rows, one number
slides.main: An aggregate function collapses many rows into one value.

captions: A regular query returns as many rows as it found
An aggregate function collapses all rows into one value
An aggregate without grouping always returns one row
COUNT(*) counts whole rows, whatever the columns contain
WHERE runs before the aggregate: only paid orders are counted
For an empty set COUNT returns 0, not a gap

slides.title: SUM and AVG
slides.main: SUM adds up, AVG divides the sum by the number of values.

captions: SUM adds up the column: 148,200 for all five orders
AVG is the sum divided by the count of values: 29,640
The mean is usually fractional: ROUND(x, 2) keeps two decimals

slides.title: MIN and MAX
slides.main: MIN and MAX work with numbers, strings and dates.

captions: MIN returns the smallest value: 3900
MAX is the largest: 79500; but the aggregate does not return the row itself
They work on strings and dates: earliest date, last name alphabetically

slides.title: COUNT(column)
slides.main: COUNT(col) counts only non-empty values of the column.

captions: COUNT(*) counts all five rows
COUNT(brand) counts only non-empty values: three
COUNT(*) − COUNT(brand) shows the number of gaps

slides.title: NULL and aggregates
slides.main: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULL; on an empty set SUM gives NULL.

captions: The mean of 10, NULL, 30 is 20: a gap is not zero and not in the divisor
With no matching rows, SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns zero
COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) turns NULL into zero
COUNT(city) counts non-empty values: four
With DISTINCT duplicates go away: Moscow, Kazan, Tver — three
DISTINCT inside an aggregate and after SELECT are different things

slides.title: WHERE and aggregates
slides.main: WHERE selects rows first, then the aggregate counts them.

captions: WHERE selects rows first, then the aggregate collapses the rest
Sum of paid orders: 55,400 + 4,200 = 59,600
A condition on an aggregate in WHERE is impossible — no sum yet; use HAVING

slides.title: Column next to aggregate
slides.main: A plain column next to an aggregate without GROUP BY is a logic error.

captions: SELECT status, COUNT(*) — one value next to a set of values
SQLite does not complain, but takes status from a random row: the result is wrong
Per-group totals come from GROUP BY (chapter 12)

slides.title: Several aggregates
slides.main: A single SELECT can compute any number of aggregates.

captions: Several aggregates in one SELECT work over the same set of rows
Give each an alias: result columns get clear names
Share = sum / sum: make one number fractional, or you get 0

lines: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(total) AS sum,

slides.title: Expressions inside
slides.main: Any expression goes inside an aggregate; AVG is not SUM / COUNT with NULL.

captions: SUM(qty * price) — revenue of the order lines
SUM(status = 'paid') — number of paid: a comparison gives 1 or 0
Without gaps AVG(x) = SUM(x) / COUNT(*); with gaps it does not

slides.title: GROUP_CONCAT
slides.main: GROUP_CONCAT glues the group's values into one string.

captions: GROUP_CONCAT glues the column's values into one string
The separator is the second argument; a comma by default
Order inside the string is not guaranteed; other databases call it string_agg

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Aggregates collapse a table; remember the five traps.

captions: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col), SUM of empty, NULL ignored, integer division, column next to aggregate
COUNT · SUM · AVG · MIN · MAX · GROUP_CONCAT — collapsing a set of rows
Next topic — joins: JOIN links tables by keys
